newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian gold -- shortcovering buzzword in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Asian gold -- shortcovering buzzword in Asia.

text.p: Shortcovering was the Friday buzzword in Asian time zones and the gold price was more likely to climb up than slide down in the near term despite bearishness lingering in the markets, gold traders in Asia said.
"I think the last two to three dollars (increase in gold prices) have basically been shortcovering," said a senior trader at an international bullion firm in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong gold opened sharply up at $353.15/65, compared to New York's Thursday close at at $351.25/75 per ounce.
"We opened with massive shortcovering from funds, they were all very eager to get their positions back in, and under $350 per ounce, there was huge buying," one Hong Kong gold trader said.
Singapore and Hong Kong traders said gold had also borrowed some short-term momentum from silver's rally.
"Silver was very active last night, it had a very sharp rally and sort of dragged gold back up as well," a Hong Kong trader said.

Hong Kong intraday trade was expected to remain above $352 per ounce, seen as the new support, and dealers said while gold prices firmed, they would push up past $354 or $355 per ounce only with great difficulty.
Gold fixed in London on Thursday at $348.00 an ounce, the lowest level since mid-September 1993.
COMEX March silver ended up 15.2 cents at $4.875 an ounce after recovering from a session low of $4.710 per ounce.
Hong Kong bullion dealers said they were encouraged by the market's quick bounce away from $348 per ounce overnight, noting it indicated strong support at that level.
While some players in the market were long, profit taking on the upside was light, dealers said, noting that the situation for shorts was not as stable.
"The shorts at this level are not very comfortable, so if market is higher, then there is a chance for some big shorts to cover their position," said a senior trader at a Hong Kong bullion house.
"I think there would be more interest to cover than interest for fresh selling," another said.
Chartists pointed to new lows as an important signal for a market reversal.
A temporary squeeze in physical supply in Hong Kong and Singapore had pushed up local premiums, but was unlikely to have an impact on gold prices, dealers in both centres said.
Spot gold premiums in Singapore had risen by 20-30 U.S. cents to around a dollar an ounce from last week, over loco London levels, dealers said.

But overall, prices remained under pressure and were likely to dip further while the U.S. dollar remained strong and continued to attract investment away from precious metals into U.S. assets, Singapore dealers said.
Traders said traditionally robust physical gold demand ahead of the Chinese New Year period had provided some good support, but this was seen as shortlived.

-- Ang Bee Lin in Singapore (65) 870 3174
